clinicalPearls: A rare Bardet-Biedl-like ciliopathy distinguished by iris coloboma rather than a retinal pigmentary dystrophy
Cardinal features are iris coloboma, obesity, postaxial polydactyly, hypogenitalism and intellectual disability
Hydrocephalus and facial dysmorphism have been described in some reports
Overlap with Bardet-Biedl and other obesity-polydactyly ciliopathies is substantial and the boundary is not always clear
The iris coloboma is the key clinical discriminator from Bardet-Biedl at presentation
Reported inheritance is autosomal recessive, though the molecular basis remains poorly defined
Diagnosis rests largely on the clinical constellation because a consistent causative gene has not been established
reference.pathophysiology: Biemond syndrome II is regarded as part of the obesity-polydactyly ciliopathy spectrum, closely resembling Bardet-Biedl syndrome but with iris coloboma in place of the usual retinal pigmentary dystrophy. Although a specific gene has not been reliably identified, the pattern of central obesity, hypogonadism, polydactyly and colobomatous eye malformation is consistent with dysfunction of the primary cilium and its role in hedgehog and other developmental signalling, as seen across the related ciliopathies. Disordered ciliary signalling during development would account for the failure of optic fissure closure that produces the coloboma, the limb patterning defect underlying postaxial polydactyly, and the hypothalamic-pituitary and central nervous system involvement reflected in obesity, hypogenitalism and intellectual disability.
additionalInvestigations: Ophthalmological assessment to confirm the iris coloboma and evaluate the retina
Radiographs of the hands and feet for postaxial polydactyly
Endocrine assessment of gonadal function and pubertal development
Renal ultrasound and function testing given the ciliopathy overlap
Developmental assessment and, where available, broad ciliopathy gene panel testing
redFlags: Progressive visual impairment prompting careful retinal evaluation
Renal impairment developing as in related ciliopathies
Endocrine deficiency affecting growth and pubertal development
reference.prognosis: Long-term outlook depends chiefly on the degree of renal and neurological involvement; historical data are limited, and management is supportive with surveillance for the complications common to related ciliopathies.
pitfalls: Assuming retinitis pigmentosa and overlooking the defining iris coloboma
Failing to look for the renal disease common to related ciliopathies
Regarding it as entirely distinct from Bardet-Biedl rather than part of a spectrum
Expecting a single diagnostic gene test to confirm the diagnosis
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: No disease-specific therapy; supportive management is modelled on the related Bardet-Biedl-type ciliopathies
Weight management through dietary and lifestyle intervention for the central obesity and its metabolic complications
Ophthalmology care for the iris coloboma, with refractive correction and visual support
Endocrine management of the hypogenitalism and hypogonadism, with hormone replacement to support pubertal development as needed
Renal surveillance with ultrasound and function testing given the ciliopathy spectrum, treating any impairment
Developmental and educational support, surgical correction of postaxial polydactyly where indicated, and management of hydrocephalus if present
Multidisciplinary care with genetic counselling for the presumed autosomal recessive inheritance
